subject: Copywriting
title: Nike: Just Do It
description: A quick, practical guide to Nike: Just Do It.

hook.text: In 1988, Nike was losing to Reebok. Three words turned the brand around. 'Just Do It' became the voice of ambition.

buildup.text: Dan Wieden drew partial inspiration from a convicted killer's last words.

discovery.text: Nike's revenue jumped from $877 million to $9.2 billion in 10 years. The slogan didn't sell shoes—it sold a mindset.

twist.text: The slogan works for running, basketball, soccer, and even wheelchair athletes.

climax.text: After 35+ years, 'Just Do It' is still used. It's the most recognized commercial slogan in the English language.

punchline.text: $877M to $9.2B. Three words did what no product could alone.

quiz.question: How much did Nike's revenue grow in the decade after 'Just Do It'?

details.summary: Nike's 'Just Do It' was created in 1988 by Dan Wieden of Wieden+Kennedy. Inspired partly by the last words of convicted murderer Gary Gilmore — 'Let's do it' — the slogan captured universal aspiration and transformed Nike from a running shoe company into a cultural icon.
details.whyItMatters: Just Do It is arguably the greatest slogan ever created. It transcends products entirely, speaking to human determination itself. It proved a slogan can define not just a brand, but a mindset.
takeaways: Dan Wieden coined the phrase in 1988 for Wieden+Kennedy
Nike's revenue soared from $877M to $9.2B in the decade after launch
The slogan works across every sport, culture, and language

faq.question: How did 'Just Do It' transform Nike's business?
faq.answer: Before 1988, Nike was losing ground to Reebok. 'Just Do It' repositioned Nike from a performance shoe brand to a lifestyle brand for anyone who aspires to push limits. Revenue grew tenfold in a decade, and Nike became the world's dominant athletic brand.

faq.question: Is it true the slogan was inspired by a murderer's last words?
faq.answer: Dan Wieden confirmed that Gary Gilmore's final words — 'Let's do it' — were part of his inspiration. He admired the blunt courage of the phrase and modified it. The dark origin is ironic given the slogan's universally positive association today.
